title: Who Migrates? Social Identity and the Limits of Climate Adaptation
content:
Abstract

Migration is increasingly framed as a key climate adaptation strategy, yet this framing often overlooks how social hierarchies structure the feasibility of migration. We investigate this relationship in South India, a critical development context characterized by high caste stratification, out-migration, and rainfall variability. We conceptualize migration as a threshold process in which household capacity increases the feasibility of moving, while social identity may constrain the translation of capacity into adaptive action. Using repeated cross-sectional data from 27,122 households linked with high-resolution rainfall data, we estimate migration responses to rainfall variability across different caste groups. We find that marginalized caste groups have substantially lower migration probabilities under normal rainfall conditions, but they become significantly more responsive as rainfall anomalies become more severe. This pattern suggests a bifurcation in adaptation behavior: while advantaged groups migrate more under typical conditions, marginalized groups are more responsive to severe rainfall stressors. Counterfactual simulations show that migration gaps persist even when household capacities are equalized. These findings suggest that adaptation inequality is not merely a problem of endowment deficits but of identity-based constraints tied to caste, requiring policies that address the structural barriers to adaptation.
